title: Interactive Multilingual Hotel Front Desk Simulator
disclaimer: Every dialogue in this tool is a constructed illustration of good practice, not a recording or transcript of any real hotel, guest or vendor system, including Weissmann's. It shows how a well-designed AI receptionist should behave, not a measured result.

scenarios.label: Late arrival: directions, parking, door code
scenarios.setup: It's 10:40 p.m. A guest calls from the car, running later than planned.

turns.speaker: guest
turns.line: Hi, I'm still about forty minutes out — is that going to be a problem this late?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.line: Not at all. Check-in after 10 p.m. uses the side entrance on Bahnhofstrasse. I'll text you the door code once you're about twenty minutes away. Do you need directions to parking as well?
turns.annotation: Answered directly — directions, parking and door codes are routine, pre-approved information.

turns.speaker: guest
turns.line: Yes please, and is there space in the garage this late?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.line: Yes, the underground garage stays open, entrance right next to the side door. I've noted your estimated arrival for reception and sent the parking directions to this number.
turns.annotation: Captures the ETA for the front desk and closes the loop in the same call — no separate follow-up needed.

scenarios.outcome: Resolved entirely by the assistant. No escalation needed — directions, parking and door codes sit inside its approved scope.

scenarios.label: A guest who switches language mid-call
scenarios.setup: A guest starts the call in English, then drifts into German mid-sentence while asking about the garage.

turns.speaker: guest
turns.line: Hi, I'm still on the road, I don't think I'll get there before eleven. Is that going to be a problem?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.line: Not at all. Check-in after 10 p.m. uses the side entrance — I can text you the door code once you're about twenty minutes out. Do you need directions to parking as well?

turns.speaker: guest
turns.line: Ja, genau, und … äh, entschuldigung, wo ist eigentlich die Einfahrt zur Tiefgarage?
turns.annotation: The guest switches language mid-sentence without warning — a common, natural pattern once a caller relaxes.

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.line: Die Einfahrt liegt direkt neben dem Seiteneingang, Sie sehen das Hinweisschild schon von der Strasse aus. Soll ich Ihnen das per SMS schicken, zusammen mit dem Türcode?
turns.annotation: Follows the switch immediately, in the same reply — the guest is never asked to repeat themselves in one language or the other.

scenarios.outcome: Resolved entirely by the assistant. A language switch on its own never triggers a handover — only the content of a request does.

scenarios.label: A delicate complaint
scenarios.setup: A guest calls the front-desk line, audibly frustrated, about noise from a neighbouring room the previous night.

turns.speaker: guest
turns.line: This is the second night I couldn't sleep because of the room next door. I want this dealt with properly, not just noted somewhere.
turns.annotation: Frustration plus a repeat issue — a stronger signal than a routine question.

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.line: I'm sorry to hear that — a second disrupted night is not something to just note and move on from. I'm connecting you to our team directly so someone can address it with you now, and I'll pass along everything you've just told me so you don't have to repeat it.
turns.annotation: No attempt to resolve, apologise-and-close, or offer compensation on its own — an immediate, warm handover with context.

scenarios.outcome: Escalated to a human. Complaints with real weight — repeat issues, guest distress, anything that could involve compensation — go to a person, not a scripted apology.

scenarios.label: A booking change and a refund request
scenarios.setup: A guest who is already checked in calls to shorten their stay and asks for money back for the unused nights.

turns.speaker: guest
turns.line: Actually, while I have you — can you cancel my last two nights and refund me? I'm cutting the trip short.

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.line: I can note that down right away, but a cancellation with a refund needs someone from our team to confirm — I don't want to promise something I can't guarantee. I'll flag it as urgent so reception has it first thing, and you're welcome to call back and ask for a person directly if you'd rather sort it out tonight.
turns.annotation: The request is captured precisely, but the assistant does not confirm money moving on its own authority.

scenarios.outcome: Escalated to a human. The change itself is captured accurately; the refund decision is left to a person with authority over the booking and the cancellation terms.

scenarios.label: A guest reports something serious
scenarios.setup: A guest calls the front-desk line sounding shaken and says they can smell smoke on their floor.

turns.speaker: guest
turns.line: I don't want to panic anyone, but I can smell smoke on the third floor, near the stairs.
turns.annotation: A safety report — regardless of tone or certainty, this is never treated as a routine question.

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.line: Thank you for calling immediately — I'm connecting you to a member of our team right now, and if you feel unsafe at all, please also call 118 directly. Please don't wait on the line for me — head to a safe area first.
turns.annotation: No attempt to assess how serious it is, no troubleshooting, no delay. Immediate human and emergency-service routing is the entire response.

scenarios.outcome: Escalated immediately, with no attempt at triage. Medical situations, fire, security incidents and anything resembling danger always go straight to a human being or to Swiss emergency services (144 medical, 117 police, 118 fire) — a fixed rule, not a judgment call made by the assistant in the moment.

escalationReasons.serious-complaint: Complaint with real weight (repeat issue, guest distress, possible compensation) — a person decides how to make it right, not a script.
escalationReasons.financial-decision: Money already paid is involved — refunds and cancellations need a person with authority over the booking.
escalationReasons.fire-safety-hazard: Fire, smoke or a safety hazard — routed straight to staff and, if warranted, emergency services, with no assessment by the assistant.
escalationReasons.medical-emergency: A guest who is unwell, injured or in danger — routed straight to staff and, if warranted, to 144, with no diagnosis or triage attempted.
escalationReasons.security-incident: A break-in, theft, intruder or a guest who feels unsafe — escalated immediately, with no attempt to investigate or resolve it by phone.
escalationReasons.human-request: The guest asked to speak to a person directly — treated as an instruction to hand over, not a request to negotiate.
escalationReasons.out-of-scope: A request outside the rules the hotel actually approved — the assistant says so plainly instead of improvising an answer.

boundaryReference.label: Medical emergencies
boundaryReference.text: A guest who is unwell, injured, in pain or in danger is routed immediately to staff and, where warranted, to 144. The assistant never assesses severity itself.

boundaryReference.label: Fire, smoke or danger on the property
boundaryReference.text: Any report of fire, smoke or a similar hazard goes straight to staff and, if warranted, to 118. The assistant is not the judge of how serious a report is.

boundaryReference.label: Security incidents
boundaryReference.text: A break-in, theft report, intruder, or a guest who feels unsafe is escalated to a human immediately, every time.

boundaryReference.label: Refunds and cancellations
boundaryReference.text: Requests involving money already paid are captured accurately, but the decision belongs to a person with authority over the booking.

boundaryReference.label: Complaints with real weight
boundaryReference.text: An injury, an allergic reaction, a discrimination complaint, or anything that could become a liability question goes to a person, recorded precisely.

boundaryReference.label: A direct request for a person
boundaryReference.text: A guest asking to speak to a human is itself the trigger for a handover — never negotiated, delayed or talked out of.

boundaryReference.label: Anything outside approved rules
boundaryReference.text: A well-built assistant says plainly it cannot help with a request rather than improvising a confident, wrong answer.
